name: A change, recorded
summary: Every change that lands carries one record, written by ocoeco while the change is made: its kind, its one-line summary, what it advances (backlog items, milestones), what it decided, the manual work it took. The commit message is rendered from the record; a release consumes the records.
why: Data produced as a side effect of the one thing every change must do cannot go stale; recording becomes the way in, not a second task.

name: Chainability
summary: One project's data can feed another's - device tests into a grand project's path, a tool's releases into a lab's - each row carrying where it came from.
why: An ecosystem, not a heap: data flows along the real relations between projects.

name: Data made by work
summary: A project's data is produced by its work - commits, builds, tests, releases - not typed up afterwards; what only a person can supply is written once, where the work happens.
why: Records kept by hand are kept late, wrong, or not at all.

name: Manual-work saturation
summary: A project's ledger of small actions done by hand, each counted. Doing one again bumps its count; past three it is saturated and asks for a tool. A record automated by a tool says so - and a later bump asks why it was done by hand again. Deliberate hand-work (looking, listening, deciding) is counted but never asks. Saturation is effort, not only count: minutes weighted by load (0-10, Borg CR10).
why: Practice 20 says build the tool when the same hand-work comes a third time; nothing counted the times. The ledger is the counter, and the observatory sums it across projects to show where one shared tool would serve many.

name: Data made by work
summary: A project's data is produced by its development and its functioning - commits, builds, tests, releases, measurements - as a principle and by tools, never kept by hand.
why: Hand-kept data goes stale and lies; data made by work is as true as the work.

name: The observatory is a mirror
summary: Projects produce their data; the observatory reads it. Everything breathes through ocoeco - its language, gatherers and checks - and no project needs the observatory to work.
why: A mirror that projects depend on becomes a single point of failure.

name: One language, so the pieces join
summary: Plain text tables, a mark, shared names for the common things (idea, path, workings, work), and data that feeds other projects' data with its origin on every line.
why: Without one language nothing can be gathered or compared.

name: Prior art travels with the ideas
summary: A project's sources are what people already learned that it stands on, and what it takes from each; concepts and decisions cite them, so the research behind an idea is seen where the idea is.
why: Asked by the author: take the best humanity has to offer into account, and let it propagate through everything.

name: Look around first
summary: Before acting: what is, what we are dealing with, why it is so, and what others already learned - kept as research (the question, what was found, its sources), cited by the decisions that rest on it, shown beside the steps those decisions are about.
why: No action is complete if it does not begin with a clear look at the situation. The chain research, decision, step lets anyone follow a step down to what it rests on.

name: Research has versions
summary: A refresh adds a new version and never overwrites; earlier versions stay one click away. Views of facts follow the latest version; a decision keeps citing the version it rested on, and says when a newer one exists.
why: A decision made on old research should say so, not silently appear to rest on new findings.

name: tad, the format
summary: Text as data - tables as JSON lines with a schema, a canonical form and verification - is the format ocoeco speaks.
why: Readable by people, diffable by git, checkable by machines.

name: Three ways of knowing
summary: Live: gathered from a marked project as its work happens - the default, unmarked. Researched: taken from outside the commons, dated, with how it was found and its sources - shown outlined, with its age, linking to the research. Unknown: neither, and said so.
why: The author: let what others achieved fill the picture so it does not look empty to a newcomer - while making plain how we know each thing, and how fresh it is.

name: A vocabulary every project speaks
summary: Each project keeps its words and their exact meaning - what a word means in plain language, what it is not, what it is easily confused with. ocoeco defines the shared words (mark, lens, essence, working, cutting, conveyor...); projects inherit them and add their own; a redefined shared word is flagged. Shown as a page, and as the terms underlined in the project's own pages with their meaning beside them.
why: Concepts say what a project rests on; a vocabulary says what its words mean. Without it the words drift into dialects and live only in the heads that coined them.
